opening.text: Think about the first time you walked into a home you were going to live in. Maybe you were a child moving to a new town. Maybe you were newly married. You stood at the front door. Someone handed you a key.
That door did not make the house yours. But it was the way in. Before you crossed it, you were a visitor. After you crossed it, you were home.

Baptism is a door like that. It is the first doorway into the kingdom of God. Before it, we may believe in Jesus Christ, and we may want to follow Him. After it, we have made a promise, and He has made a promise to us. We are no longer standing outside.
I want to talk about that door today. Why Jesus walked through it first. Why we walk through it too. And what it means to live in the house after we enter.
Baptism is not just something we did when we were eight, or something we watch a friend do. It is something we can think about and renew all our lives.

mainMessage.text: Baptism is the doorway to Christ's kingdom. Jesus showed us the way, and when we go down into the water and come up again, we make a covenant with God and begin a new life.

blocks.text: Let's start with who went first.
Jesus Christ had no sin. He did not need to be forgiven of anything. And yet He walked to the River Jordan to be baptized by John. John was surprised. He tried to talk Him out of it.

Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
Look at who is present. The Son is in the water. The Holy Ghost comes down like a dove. The Father speaks from heaven. All three are there. It is a sacred moment, and the Father says He is pleased.
Nephi, who lived 600 years earlier, saw this in vision and explained why it mattered.

And now, if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness, O then, how much more need have we, being unholy, to be baptized, yea, even by water! And now, I would ask of you, my beloved brethren, wherein the Lamb of God did fulfil all righteousness in being baptized by water? Know ye not that he was holy? But notwithstanding he being holy, he showeth unto the children of men that, according to the flesh he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments.

How much more need have we. That is the question that settles it for me. If the holy Son of God chose to be baptized, I do not need to wonder whether I should. He set the pattern. He showed me what obedience looks like.
So why is baptism needed? The Savior explained it to a man named Nicodemus, a leader who came to Him at night.
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
Born of water and of the Spirit. Two parts. We are baptized in water. Then we receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. Together they make a new birth.
After Peter's powerful sermon on the day of Pentecost, the crowd asked what to do. His answer was short and clear.

Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
See the order. Repent. Be baptized. Receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. And the result is the remission of sins. That means our sins are forgiven.
Elder David A. Bednar spoke about what happens after the water. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

Hence, as we are born again and strive to always have His Spirit to be with us, the Holy Ghost sanctifies and refines our souls as if by fire (see 2 Nephi 31:13–14, 17). Ultimately, we are to stand spotless before God.
That is the promise. The water is the start. Then the Spirit keeps cleaning and shaping us, day by day. Baptism opens the door, and the Holy Ghost goes with us through the house.
Why do we go under the water? What is the picture?
The apostle Paul gave us the picture.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.

We are buried. We are raised. That is the shape of baptism by immersion. When we go under the water, it is like the burial of the old way of living. When we come up, it is like the resurrection of Jesus. We walk in newness of life.
This is not a small change. Elder David A. Bednar explained it in his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference:

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon “the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah” (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.
To be spiritually reborn. Not just to have a ceremony. To be changed.

If you remember your own baptism, you may recall a feeling of being clean. For many, it is one of the clearest memories of childhood. If you were baptized later in life, you may remember the feeling of finally stepping through. Either way, hold on to it. That feeling points to something real. It is the beginning of a new life with Christ.
A door leads somewhere. What is inside the house of baptism?
A covenant. That is a sacred promise between us and God. When Alma taught at the waters of Mormon, he told the people what they were really agreeing to.

Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?

I love how this reads. It is not a list of rules. It is a description of the kind of people we want to be. People who carry each other's burdens. People who mourn with those who mourn. People who comfort. And in return, God pours out His Spirit more abundantly.
In our day, the Lord gave a clear description of who is ready for baptism.

And again, by way of commandment to the church concerning the manner of baptism—All those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized, and come forth with broken hearts and contrite spirits, and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end, and truly manifest by their works that they have received of the Spirit of Christ unto the remission of their sins, shall be received by baptism into his church.
A humble heart. A willingness to repent. A desire to take on His name. A determination to serve Him to the end. Those are the marks of someone walking through the door.
Notice the words "to the end." Baptism is not a single day. It is a promise for a lifetime.
Now I want to speak about the how. The Savior was careful about the way baptism is done.
When He appeared to the Nephites, He gave them exact instructions.

Verily I say unto you, that whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name, on this wise shall ye baptize them—Behold, ye shall go down and stand in the water, and in my name shall ye baptize them. And now behold, these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name, saying: Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And then shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water.
Three things stand out. The person is baptized by someone who has authority. The person is called by name. And the person is fully immersed in the water.

Why does this matter? Because baptism is not a symbol we invent. It is an ordinance the Lord set. He gives the authority through His priesthood. He decides how it is done. That is why a baptism in our Church is performed by someone holding the priesthood, and why baptisms performed without that authority are not the same.
And He gave a promise to those who take this step.
And whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved; and they are they who shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Anyone who believes and is baptized. Not only those who grew up in the Church. Anyone. The door is open to every child of God.
Here is something that surprises many people. Baptism is not a one-time promise we then forget. The Lord gives us a way to renew it every week.
When we take the sacrament, we promise the same things we promised in the water. We take His name. We remember Him. We keep His commandments. And we are promised that we may always have His Spirit.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him and keep his commandments which he has given them; that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks tied the two together. In his talk "Always Have His Spirit," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

. . . Out of the seemingly small act of consciously and reverently renewing our baptismal covenants comes a renewal of the blessings of baptism by water and by the Spirit, that we may always have his Spirit to be with us. In this way all of us will be guided, and in this way all of us can be cleansed.
A seemingly small act. A bite of bread. A sip of water. But it brings us back to the doorway each week.
Elder Bednar said baptism is the beginning of a life, not the end of a task. In "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he taught:

. . . After we come out of the waters of baptism, our souls need to be continuously immersed in and saturated with the truth and the light of the Savior’s gospel. Sporadic and shallow dipping in the doctrine of Christ and partial participation in His restored Church cannot produce the spiritual transformation that enables us to walk in a newness of life. Rather, fidelity to covenants, constancy of commitment, and offering our whole soul unto God are required if we are to receive the blessings of eternity. . . . Total immersion in and saturation with the Savior’s gospel are essential steps in the process of being born again.
It does not say we must be perfect. It says we must be immersed. Stay in the water, so to speak.
And Elder D. Todd Christofferson gave comfort to those who feel they have not changed fast enough. In his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference, he said:

You may ask, Why doesn’t this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
It is a process. If you are still working on it, you are in good company. That is what life in the house looks like.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about their own baptism, or a baptism they saw. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The Ethiopian official is baptized

blocks.text: Philip was a disciple who met an official from Ethiopia on a desert road. The man was reading the book of Isaiah and did not understand it. Philip explained that it spoke of Jesus. Then something happened.

And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized? And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him. And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing.
He saw the water, and he asked what stood in the way. Nothing did. He went down, he came up, and he went on rejoicing. That is the doorway, and the joy on the other side.

application.text: Here are three things to try this week.
First, remember your baptism. Find the date. Think about who was there and how you felt. If you can, look at a photo or a certificate. Let the memory remind you of the promise.
Second, pay attention at the sacrament. Instead of letting your mind drift, think of one promise you made at baptism and ask how you kept it this week.
Third, if you know someone who is not baptized, pray for a chance to share what it means to you. Do not push. Just be open. The door is for everyone.

blocks.text: I know that baptism is the doorway to a new life. I know that Jesus Christ showed us the way. I have felt the Spirit as I have tried to keep the promises I made. I know the Lord keeps His promises too. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

You will have His Spirit to be with you always.

closingVerse.text: For the gate by which ye should enter is repentance and baptism by water; and then cometh a remission of your sins by fire and by the Holy Ghost.

opening.text: A wedding ring is a small thing. A little circle of metal. You could buy one for a few dollars. It does not do much on its own.

But put it on the hand of someone who has just made a promise, and it means everything. It says, I belong to someone. It says, I have made a vow, and I intend to keep it. It reminds that person every day, every time they glance down.

Baptism is like that. The water itself is just water. A pool, a font, a river. But when a person goes down into it after repenting and believing in Jesus Christ, it becomes a sign of a promise. The person says to God, I am yours. And God says, I am yours too.
Today I want to talk about that promise. Where it began, why it matters, and how we can wear it every day, the way a ring is worn.
I will share what Jesus did, what the scriptures say baptism does for us, and what we promise when we step into the water.

mainMessage.text: Baptism is a covenant, a two-way promise with God. Jesus Christ set the example, and when we are baptized and receive the Holy Ghost, we are born again into a new life with Him.

blocks.text: The first thing to know is that Jesus did it first.
He did not send others into the water while He stood on the bank. He went Himself. He walked to the Jordan and asked John to baptize Him.

Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
Heaven opened. The Spirit came down. The Father spoke. Whenever someone says baptism is just a formality, I think of this scene. It was anything but a formality.
Why did the sinless Son of God do this? Nephi gave the answer.

And now, if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness, O then, how much more need have we, being unholy, to be baptized, yea, even by water! And now, I would ask of you, my beloved brethren, wherein the Lamb of God did fulfil all righteousness in being baptized by water? Know ye not that he was holy? But notwithstanding he being holy, he showeth unto the children of men that, according to the flesh he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments.
Obedience. Humility. A witness to the Father. If He needed to show those, we certainly do. When we follow Him into the water, we say, I want to be like You.
What does baptism do for us? The scriptures give a clear and simple answer.
Nicodemus came to Jesus by night. He was a learned man. And the Savior told him something that must have surprised him.
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

Born of water and of the Spirit. A birth is a beginning. You do not choose to be born the first time. But you do choose this second birth. That is what makes baptism a covenant. It is something we say yes to.
On the day of Pentecost, a crowd had just heard that they had rejected the Son of God. They were deeply troubled.

Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
What shall we do? A question every honest heart asks. And the answer was not complicated. Repent. Be baptized. Receive the Holy Ghost.
Elder David A. Bednar said what that Holy Ghost then does in us. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

Hence, as we are born again and strive to always have His Spirit to be with us, the Holy Ghost sanctifies and refines our souls as if by fire (see 2 Nephi 31:13–14, 17). Ultimately, we are to stand spotless before God.
The ring goes on at the baptism. But the work of becoming spotless is a lifetime of the Spirit's help. We do not do it on our own.
What is the picture that baptism paints? The apostle Paul explains it in his letter to the Romans.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.

This tells me why immersion matters. We go down. We come up. It reminds us of the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. And then Paul says: walk in newness of life. Not just feel new, but walk new. Live new.
Elder Bednar helped many of us understand what that change really is. In his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon “the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah” (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.
Notice who does the heavy lifting. It is made possible through the merits, mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah. We do not change by gritting our teeth. We change as we lean on Him.
Think of a ring that has been worn for many years. It becomes part of the hand. In the same way, a life lived under this covenant slowly becomes part of who we are.
Every ring stands for a vow. What is the vow of baptism?
Alma spelled it out for a group of people who had come to hear him teach in the wilderness. They wanted to join the people of God. He asked them what they were willing to do.

Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
This is a vow about people. Bear burdens. Mourn with the sad. Comfort the lonely. Be a witness. It is a vow about how we treat the people around us, and how we show up for God.
And there is a promise on God's side. He will pour out His Spirit more abundantly. In every real covenant, both sides give something.
In modern revelation, the Lord described who is ready to take this vow.

And again, by way of commandment to the church concerning the manner of baptism—All those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized, and come forth with broken hearts and contrite spirits, and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end, and truly manifest by their works that they have received of the Spirit of Christ unto the remission of their sins, shall be received by baptism into his church.

A broken heart and a contrite spirit. Willing to take His name. Determined to serve to the end. When you wear a ring, you are saying that you are not going to take it off. This is the same. To the end.
Who can perform this ordinance, and how? The Lord was very specific, and for good reason.
When the risen Savior visited the people in the Americas, He told His twelve disciples exactly what to say.

Verily I say unto you, that whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name, on this wise shall ye baptize them—Behold, ye shall go down and stand in the water, and in my name shall ye baptize them. And now behold, these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name, saying: Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And then shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water.
The person is called by name. The one baptizing has authority from Jesus Christ. The words are the same each time. And the person is immersed.

Imagine a wedding conducted by someone with no authority to marry. The couple might be sincere, but the marriage would not be legal. In a much more important way, baptism needs the Lord's authority to count. That is why priesthood is so important in this work.
And a promise follows for every person who takes this step.
And whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved; and they are they who shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Whoso. That word means anyone. Old or young. New to faith or a long-time believer. Whoever believes and is baptized.
Here is the question I find most important. How do I keep this covenant fresh, so it does not become a thing I did long ago?
A ring may sit on a finger for forty years. But a good marriage is not kept alive by the ring. It is kept alive by choices each day. The same is true of baptism.
The Lord gave us the sacrament so that we renew the covenant every week.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him and keep his commandments which he has given them; that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.
Listen to the words. Take His name. Always remember Him. Keep His commandments. Always have His Spirit. These are the promises of baptism, spoken again.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks said it well in his talk "Always Have His Spirit," from the October 1996 general conference:

. . . Out of the seemingly small act of consciously and reverently renewing our baptismal covenants comes a renewal of the blessings of baptism by water and by the Spirit, that we may always have his Spirit to be with us. In this way all of us will be guided, and in this way all of us can be cleansed.
Consciously. Reverently. That is the secret. It is not about the bread. It is about how we think while we take it.
Elder Bednar, in "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, described how deep our commitment should go:

. . . After we come out of the waters of baptism, our souls need to be continuously immersed in and saturated with the truth and the light of the Savior’s gospel. Sporadic and shallow dipping in the doctrine of Christ and partial participation in His restored Church cannot produce the spiritual transformation that enables us to walk in a newness of life. Rather, fidelity to covenants, constancy of commitment, and offering our whole soul unto God are required if we are to receive the blessings of eternity. . . . Total immersion in and saturation with the Savior’s gospel are essential steps in the process of being born again.
A ring is worn all the time, not just on Sundays. This is how Elder Bednar describes our discipleship. Constant. Whole. Not sporadic.
Finally, Elder D. Todd Christofferson said something for the person who thinks, "I am not changing fast enough." In his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference, he said:

You may ask, Why doesn’t this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
A process. Like a ring that gets worn smooth over time. Be patient. Keep going.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about their own baptism, or a baptism they saw. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Alma baptizes at the waters of Mormon

blocks.text: A prophet named Alma had fled from a wicked king. He taught people secretly, and hundreds believed. At a quiet pool called the waters of Mormon, he began to baptize them.

And now it came to pass that Alma took Helam, he being one of the first, and went and stood forth in the water, and cried, saying: O Lord, pour out thy Spirit upon thy servant, that he may do this work with holiness of heart. And when he had said these words, the Spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he said: Helam, I baptize thee, having authority from the Almighty God, as a testimony that ye have entered into a covenant to serve him until you are dead as to the mortal body; and may the Spirit of the Lord be poured out upon you; and may he grant unto you eternal life, through the redemption of Christ, whom he has prepared from the foundation of the world. And after Alma had said these words, both Alma and Helam were buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing, being filled with the Spirit. And again, Alma took another, and went forth a second time into the water, and baptized him according to the first, only he did not bury himself again in the water. And after this manner he did baptize every one that went forth to the place of Mormon; and they were in number about two hundred and four souls; yea, and they were baptized in the waters of Mormon, and were filled with the grace of God.

Notice that Alma prayed first. He asked for the Spirit so that he could do this work with holiness of heart. And notice what happened next. They came out rejoicing. They were filled with the Spirit. And about two hundred and four people were baptized there.

application.text: Here are a few simple ways to live this out.
Think of baptism as a ring. When did you last look at yours? Take a few quiet minutes this week to think about the promise you made. Write down one part of it that you want to do better.
When you take the sacrament, try this. Before the bread comes, pick one covenant word. Take. Remember. Keep. Spirit. Let that word guide your thoughts.
And if someone near you is thinking about baptism, welcome them. Offer to go with them to a service. You may be the person who helps them put on the ring.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that baptism is real and that the promise is real on both sides. I know that Jesus Christ was baptized to show us the way. I have felt the Holy Ghost guide me when I have tried to keep my covenants. I know He keeps His part. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to take a few quiet minutes this week to think about the promise you made at baptism. Write down one part you want to do better.
I invite you to choose one covenant word before the sacrament: Take, Remember, Keep or Spirit. Let that word guide your thoughts.
I invite you to welcome someone who is thinking about baptism. Offer to go with them to a service.
blessings: You will see more clearly where you can grow.
You will take the sacrament with more meaning, and the Spirit will be with you.
You will share in the joy of someone beginning a covenant with God.

closingVerse.text: If ye love me, keep my commandments.

opening.text: Have you ever watched a citizenship ceremony? A room full of people from many countries stand together. Some of them waited for years. They studied. They filled out forms. They passed tests. Then one day they raise their right hands and make a promise to their new country.
When it is over, something has changed. They have the same faces, the same names, the same stories. But they now belong. They have rights they did not have before. They carry a new name: citizen.

Baptism has something of that feeling. We come from many places. We have made many mistakes. And Jesus Christ says, there is a way to belong. Come, take My name. Make a promise. Become a citizen of My kingdom.
The apostle Paul told new believers, "Ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Ephesians 2:19). That is what happens at baptism.
I want to speak about how we get there. The example Christ set, what baptism does, and the promises we make as new citizens of His kingdom.

mainMessage.text: In baptism, we take the name of Jesus Christ and join His kingdom. He set the example, He gives us power through the Holy Ghost, and He asks us to live as His people all our lives.

blocks.text: Let's look at the first citizen of the kingdom. Jesus Himself.
He came to the Jordan River and asked John to baptize Him. John felt it should be the other way around.

Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
"To fulfil all righteousness." That phrase means to do everything that God requires. Jesus showed that no one is exempt. And He showed it in front of witnesses, with heaven's approval.
Nephi explained the reasoning with a simple argument.

And now, if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness, O then, how much more need have we, being unholy, to be baptized, yea, even by water! And now, I would ask of you, my beloved brethren, wherein the Lamb of God did fulfil all righteousness in being baptized by water? Know ye not that he was holy? But notwithstanding he being holy, he showeth unto the children of men that, according to the flesh he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments.
If He did it, how much more should we. It is an argument that needs no long explanation. When the leader goes first, the rest of us follow.
Now, what does baptism actually do? Jesus explained it plainly to a man named Nicodemus.
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
There it is. The entrance to the kingdom. Water and Spirit. Like a country with a gate, and two keys. We cannot skip either one.
Peter said much the same on the day of Pentecost.

Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Three things come to us here. We repent. We are baptized. And we receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. The first is our change of heart. The second is the covenant. The third is the power to live it.
Elder David A. Bednar described what that Spirit does for the new citizen. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

Hence, as we are born again and strive to always have His Spirit to be with us, the Holy Ghost sanctifies and refines our souls as if by fire (see 2 Nephi 31:13–14, 17). Ultimately, we are to stand spotless before God.
The Holy Ghost is like a guide who knows the laws and the roads of the new country. He teaches us, corrects us, and cleans us up as we go.
What does it mean to be born again? Paul gave the most vivid picture.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.
We go into the water as the old person. We come out as the new. It is a burial and a resurrection in a single act.
That is why the ceremony cannot be done halfway. The old life is laid down, and the new life is taken up.
Elder Bednar helped us see the depth of this. In his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon “the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah” (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.
Fundamental and permanent. A new citizen does not go back to the old country on weekends. We are changed, and we live that way.
And the change is not by our own strength. It is made possible through the merits, mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah. That means we can start, even when we feel weak. We are not doing this alone.
When a person becomes a citizen, they make a pledge. What is the pledge of baptism?
Alma gave the clearest description at the waters of Mormon. He asked the people a series of questions, and each one was a promise.

Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?

Look at the first line. Come into the fold of God. Be called his people. This is the language of belonging. And the duties of this citizenship are tender. Carry one another's burdens. Mourn with those who mourn. Comfort those who need it.
A good citizen does not only protect their own rights. They look after their neighbors. And so does a disciple.
The Lord describes who is ready for this in our own day.

And again, by way of commandment to the church concerning the manner of baptism—All those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized, and come forth with broken hearts and contrite spirits, and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end, and truly manifest by their works that they have received of the Spirit of Christ unto the remission of their sins, shall be received by baptism into his church.
Take upon them the name of Jesus Christ. That is the pledge at the heart of it. We take His name. We are known by it. And we try to live in a way that does honor to it.
A citizenship ceremony has an official in charge. Someone who has the authority to say, you are now one of us. Baptism has that too.
The Savior gave His disciples the exact words they were to use.

Verily I say unto you, that whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name, on this wise shall ye baptize them—Behold, ye shall go down and stand in the water, and in my name shall ye baptize them. And now behold, these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name, saying: Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And then shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water.
Having authority given me of Jesus Christ. That line is not decoration. It is the heart of why this ordinance is valid. The priesthood is the authority God gives to His servants to act in His name.
It also means the person being baptized receives a witness, a testimony from heaven, that the promise is real. The words are the same, whether in a font in a city or a river in the countryside.
And He gave this promise.
And whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved; and they are they who shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Inherit the kingdom of God. That is what citizens do. They inherit rights and blessings. And the Savior invites everyone to claim them.
Now, a citizen has to live in the country. A citizenship certificate means nothing if you never show up.
So how do we live our baptism? One of the best ways is the sacrament. Each week we renew the promises we made.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him and keep his commandments which he has given them; that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.
Every Sunday, we say, again, that we are willing to take His name. Every Sunday, we hear the promise that we may always have His Spirit.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks taught how this works. In his talk "Always Have His Spirit," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

. . . Out of the seemingly small act of consciously and reverently renewing our baptismal covenants comes a renewal of the blessings of baptism by water and by the Spirit, that we may always have his Spirit to be with us. In this way all of us will be guided, and in this way all of us can be cleansed.
Guided and cleansed. Two gifts that come from small, reverent acts, done again and again.
Elder Bednar gave a challenge about how fully to live this. In his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

. . . After we come out of the waters of baptism, our souls need to be continuously immersed in and saturated with the truth and the light of the Savior’s gospel. Sporadic and shallow dipping in the doctrine of Christ and partial participation in His restored Church cannot produce the spiritual transformation that enables us to walk in a newness of life. Rather, fidelity to covenants, constancy of commitment, and offering our whole soul unto God are required if we are to receive the blessings of eternity. . . . Total immersion in and saturation with the Savior’s gospel are essential steps in the process of being born again.
A citizen who lives in the country every day knows its roads and its people. A disciple who lives in the gospel every day knows the Lord's voice and His ways.
And Elder D. Todd Christofferson offered patience to those who feel behind. In his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference, he said:

You may ask, Why doesn’t this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
New citizens take time to feel at home. The same is true here. If you are still learning, you are right on schedule.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about their own baptism, or a baptism they saw. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Cornelius and his household

blocks.text: Cornelius was a Roman officer who prayed and gave to the poor. God sent Peter to teach him and his family. While Peter was still speaking, something happened that surprised everyone.

While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word. And they of the circumcision which believed were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost. For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God. Then answered Peter, Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we? And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Then prayed they him to tarry certain days.

Peter asked a simple question. Can anyone forbid water? The answer was no. Anyone who has a believing heart is welcome in the kingdom. A Roman officer, a stranger to most of Peter's friends, became a fellowcitizen that day.

application.text: Here are a few things you can do this week.
Think about your name. When you introduce yourself, you say your name. In baptism, we also take His name. Choose one way to act this week that would make His name proud.
Next, prepare for the sacrament. Before the meeting, take a quiet minute and ask, "What have I done this week that fits my promise? What could I do better?"
Finally, look around for someone who feels like a stranger at church or in the neighborhood. Say hello. Sit with them. Help them feel that they belong.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that baptism is the way into Christ's kingdom. I know that He is the Son of God and that He set the example. I have felt that promise renewed in my own life, and I have seen the Spirit confirm it. I testify that the door is open to everyone. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to choose one way to act this week that honors the name of Jesus Christ, which you took upon you at baptism.
I invite you to prepare for the sacrament by asking, "What have I done this week that fits my promise? What could I do better?"
I invite you to look for someone who feels like a stranger at church or in the neighborhood. Say hello and sit with them.
blessings: You will feel what it means to belong to Jesus Christ.
You will take the sacrament ready to renew your covenant.
Someone will feel that they belong, and you will feel it too.

closingVerse.text: For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

opening.text: A seed does not look like much. A brown speck in the palm of your hand. You might think it is dead. But plant it, and something remarkable happens.

First, the seed goes into the ground. It is buried. It is covered with dirt, and for a while nothing seems to happen. The old seed is gone. Then a small green shoot pushes up through the soil. A new thing has come out of the old.
A farmer knows this rhythm. Burial, then life. Every gardener trusts it.
The apostle Paul used this picture when he talked about baptism. He said we are planted together with Christ. We go down into the water as the seed goes into the soil. And we come up into a new life.
Today I want to talk about the seed and the water. We will look at what Jesus did, what baptism gives us, and how to help the new life grow after we come out of the water.

mainMessage.text: Baptism buries the old life and plants us in Christ so that new life can grow. Through the Holy Ghost and the covenants we keep, that life can keep growing every day.

blocks.text: The first planting was done by the Savior Himself.
He asked John to baptize Him in the Jordan. John did not want to. Jesus insisted.

Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
When He came up out of the water, heaven opened. The Father said He was pleased. That is how a good planting begins.
Nephi, in the Book of Mormon, explained what Jesus was teaching by this.

And now, if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness, O then, how much more need have we, being unholy, to be baptized, yea, even by water! And now, I would ask of you, my beloved brethren, wherein the Lamb of God did fulfil all righteousness in being baptized by water? Know ye not that he was holy? But notwithstanding he being holy, he showeth unto the children of men that, according to the flesh he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments.
He was obedient. He was humble. And He did it in public, so we would know what to do. How much more need have we. That says it all.
A seed is planted so that something can grow. What does baptism help to grow in us?
Jesus told Nicodemus that new life starts with a second birth.
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

Water and Spirit. Like soil and sunlight. A seed needs both. If you have ever grown a plant, you know that water alone is not enough. The light has to reach it. In baptism, the water comes first, then the gift of the Holy Ghost.
On the day of Pentecost, when thousands wanted to know how to begin, Peter's answer was clear.

Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Repent. Be baptized. Receive the Holy Ghost. That is the full planting. And through it, our sins are forgiven. The soil is cleaned.
Elder David A. Bednar spoke about the long work of the Holy Ghost after baptism. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

Hence, as we are born again and strive to always have His Spirit to be with us, the Holy Ghost sanctifies and refines our souls as if by fire (see 2 Nephi 31:13–14, 17). Ultimately, we are to stand spotless before God.
That is the growing season. The Spirit is the sunlight that stays with us. Day after day, He shapes us.
So why does the planting involve going under the water?
Paul put it this way, and I think of a seed every time I read it.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.
Buried. Planted. Raised. The picture is full of life. We are buried with Christ, and we are raised with Him to walk in newness of life. Our old way is laid down. A new way begins.
Elder Bednar helped us understand how deep this goes. In his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon “the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah” (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.

A farmer does not make the seed grow. He plants, waters, and waits. The growing itself is a gift. In the same way, the change in us is made possible by the Holy Messiah. Our part is to stay in the soil, to keep choosing Him.
That is why baptism is a beginning. A seed in the ground is not a finished tree. But it is a start, and it is a hopeful one.
A seed has a purpose. So does a covenant. What is the purpose of the promise we make at baptism?
Alma taught it to a group of believers who had gathered by a pool of water in the wilderness. He asked them what was in their hearts.

Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
This is a garden where people grow together. Bear burdens. Mourn with those who mourn. Comfort. Be witnesses. And in return, God pours out His Spirit more abundantly, like a gentle rain.
See how the covenant is about the people around us, too. A seed in a field grows best among others. The roots of a forest reach and touch. The people of God do the same.
The Lord told the Saints in our day who is ready for this.

And again, by way of commandment to the church concerning the manner of baptism—All those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized, and come forth with broken hearts and contrite spirits, and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end, and truly manifest by their works that they have received of the Spirit of Christ unto the remission of their sins, shall be received by baptism into his church.
Broken hearts and contrite spirits. That is soft soil. A seed cannot take root in hard ground. When we come humble and ready, the Lord can do His work in us.
Who plants the seed, and how? The Lord is clear.
When the Savior appeared to the Nephites, He gave His disciples the exact words and the exact way.

Verily I say unto you, that whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name, on this wise shall ye baptize them—Behold, ye shall go down and stand in the water, and in my name shall ye baptize them. And now behold, these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name, saying: Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And then shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water.

This verse tells us three things. The words are the same every time. The person is baptized by someone with authority from Jesus Christ. And the baptism is by immersion. That matches the picture Paul gave us of burial and rising.
A good gardener plants at the right depth and the right time. The Lord gave us the pattern, and we follow it. Then we can trust that He will honor what we do.
He also gave a promise.
And whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved; and they are they who shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Whoso. That means everyone. This seed can be planted in any life, at any age, in any country.
Now comes the long season of growing. A seed does not become a tree overnight. And a baptism does not end with the day.
The Lord gave us a weekly way to care for the covenant. It is the sacrament.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him and keep his commandments which he has given them; that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.
We renew the promise. And we receive the promise again that we may always have His Spirit. Like water for a plant, we need it often.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks explained it in his talk "Always Have His Spirit," from the October 1996 general conference:

. . . Out of the seemingly small act of consciously and reverently renewing our baptismal covenants comes a renewal of the blessings of baptism by water and by the Spirit, that we may always have his Spirit to be with us. In this way all of us will be guided, and in this way all of us can be cleansed.
Small, regular acts. They add up to a strong plant.
Elder Bednar described how steady the growth should be. In his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

. . . After we come out of the waters of baptism, our souls need to be continuously immersed in and saturated with the truth and the light of the Savior’s gospel. Sporadic and shallow dipping in the doctrine of Christ and partial participation in His restored Church cannot produce the spiritual transformation that enables us to walk in a newness of life. Rather, fidelity to covenants, constancy of commitment, and offering our whole soul unto God are required if we are to receive the blessings of eternity. . . . Total immersion in and saturation with the Savior’s gospel are essential steps in the process of being born again.
A plant that is watered only now and then will wither. A plant given steady care will flourish.
And for those who worry that they are slow-growing, Elder D. Todd Christofferson shared a kind word. In his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference, he said:

You may ask, Why doesn’t this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
Growth takes time. You are not behind. You are growing.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about their own baptism, or a baptism they saw. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The jailer at Philippi

blocks.text: Paul and Silas were put in prison in the city of Philippi. In the night, an earthquake shook the building open. The jailer was frightened and ran to them. He asked a question.

And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. And they spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway. And when he had brought them into his house, he set meat before them, and rejoiced, believing in God with all his house.

The jailer went from fear to faith within a few hours. He washed the wounds of the men he had locked up. Then he was baptized, he and his whole household. And they rejoiced. A hard heart became soft ground overnight.

application.text: Here are a few ideas to try this week.
First, think of the seed. What is one small way you could care for your baptismal covenant this week? Choose something simple, such as a daily prayer, or a few minutes of scripture reading.
Second, at the sacrament, think about growth. Ask, "What has grown in me since last Sunday?" and "What needs water?"
Third, look for someone who is newly baptized. Offer them a ride, a seat, a kind word. New plants need extra care.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that baptism is a new beginning. I know that Jesus Christ walked into the water first, and that He invites us to follow. I have felt the Holy Ghost nourish and guide me as I have tried to live my covenant. I know that He helps us grow. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to choose one small way to care for your baptismal covenant this week, such as a daily prayer or a few minutes of scripture study.
I invite you to ask yourself at the sacrament, "What has grown in me since last Sunday? What needs water?"
I invite you to find someone who is newly baptized. Offer them a ride, a seat or a kind word.
blessings: Your faith will grow a little every day.
You will see how God has been helping you grow.
A new member will be nourished, and your ward or branch will be stronger.

closingVerse.text: Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

opening.text: At the start of many hiking trails, there is a wooden sign and a small box. The sign shows the map. The box holds a notebook where hikers write their names before they go. It is a simple thing. You sign your name, you note the date, and you set out.

Why do people do it? So that someone knows you started. So that if anything goes wrong, someone knows where to look. And, for many hikers, because it feels good to make a commitment before the first step.

Baptism is a little like that trailhead. It is the place where we say, I am setting out. It is where we write our name, in a way, in the book of the Lord's people. And we make a promise about the direction we plan to go.
The path is long. It goes uphill at times. But we do not walk it alone. The One who walked it first goes with us.
Today I want to talk about that starting point. What Jesus did at the Jordan, what baptism means for the journey, and how we keep walking after the first step.

mainMessage.text: Baptism is the first step on the path of discipleship. Jesus showed us the way, and through the covenant and the gift of the Holy Ghost, we are given what we need to keep going to the end.

blocks.text: Let's look at the first footprints on this trail. They belong to Jesus.
He walked to the Jordan River to be baptized. John, who had been sent to prepare the way, did not think it made sense.

Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him. And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
It is worth noticing what happens right after. The heavens open. The Holy Ghost descends. The Father speaks. The first step on the path is met with a blessing from all three.
Nephi explained why this mattered for us.

And now, if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized by water, to fulfil all righteousness, O then, how much more need have we, being unholy, to be baptized, yea, even by water! And now, I would ask of you, my beloved brethren, wherein the Lamb of God did fulfil all righteousness in being baptized by water? Know ye not that he was holy? But notwithstanding he being holy, he showeth unto the children of men that, according to the flesh he humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments.
He showeth unto the children of men. That is the key. His baptism was a lesson. He was saying to every one of us, this is how it begins.
What do we receive at the trailhead? The Savior told Nicodemus that something real and new is given.
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
There is a way in, and it has two parts. Water and Spirit. We cannot enter without both. And that is a gift of the plan of God, not a rule meant to hold us back.
On the day of Pentecost, thousands asked what to do.

Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

See what Peter says. Repent. Be baptized. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. In a trailhead sense, that is the map and the guide. We are forgiven, and we are given a Companion for the road.
Elder David A. Bednar described how that Companion works. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

Hence, as we are born again and strive to always have His Spirit to be with us, the Holy Ghost sanctifies and refines our souls as if by fire (see 2 Nephi 31:13–14, 17). Ultimately, we are to stand spotless before God.
Sanctifies and refines. A good guide does more than point. He helps you become stronger as you walk. And at the end, spotless. That is where the trail leads.
Now, why do we go all the way under the water?
Because the picture matters. Paul explained it to the Saints in Rome.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.

We go down, and the old life goes with us. We come up, and a new life begins. And then comes the instruction: walk. Walk in newness of life. That is a trail word. A walking word. It tells us that baptism is not a place to stand. It is a place to start.
Elder Bednar said this beautifully in his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference:

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon “the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah” (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.
We choose to be changed. That is the decision at the trailhead. And the power to change is not ours alone. It comes through the merits, mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah.
When the path gets steep, that is what we hold on to. We are not walking by our own strength. We are being carried, in part, by His.
At a trailhead, you sign your name and pick a direction. What are we signing up for at baptism?
Alma laid it out for the people at the waters of Mormon. They wanted to follow God, and he wanted them to know what that meant.

Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
We walk this trail with others. We bear their burdens. We mourn with them. We comfort them. And we keep walking, even until death.
That last phrase puts the length of the trail in view. It is not a short hike. It is a lifelong journey. But it is meant to be walked in company, with His Spirit poured out more abundantly.
In our day, the Lord told us what kind of traveler He is looking for.

And again, by way of commandment to the church concerning the manner of baptism—All those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized, and come forth with broken hearts and contrite spirits, and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end, and truly manifest by their works that they have received of the Spirit of Christ unto the remission of their sins, shall be received by baptism into his church.
A humble spirit. A true desire. A determination to serve to the end. Notice that it does not say a perfect record. It says repentance and a heart set in the right direction.
Who records the start, and how is it done? The Savior set a clear pattern.
When He visited the people in the Americas, He told His disciples what to say and how to do it.

Verily I say unto you, that whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name, on this wise shall ye baptize them—Behold, ye shall go down and stand in the water, and in my name shall ye baptize them. And now behold, these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name, saying: Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And then shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water.

Having authority given me of Jesus Christ. This line is why baptism is valid. The one performing it holds the priesthood, which is the authority God gives. It is the same pattern every time, in every land.
The Lord also gave a promise to those who set out.
And whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved; and they are they who shall inherit the kingdom of God.
That is the destination. The kingdom of God. And the promise is for whoever believes and is baptized. The trailhead is open to all.
Every hiker knows that the first mile is not the hard part. The hard part is mile fifteen, when you are tired and the top seems far away.
That is where the sacrament comes in. Each week, we stop, rest, and look at the map. We renew our promise.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it, that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him and keep his commandments which he has given them; that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.
We renew the promise to take His name. We promise to remember Him. And we receive the promise that we may always have His Spirit. That is a refill of water and strength on a long hike.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks taught this in his talk "Always Have His Spirit," from the October 1996 general conference:

. . . Out of the seemingly small act of consciously and reverently renewing our baptismal covenants comes a renewal of the blessings of baptism by water and by the Spirit, that we may always have his Spirit to be with us. In this way all of us will be guided, and in this way all of us can be cleansed.
Guided and cleansed. That is what a long walk with the Spirit does.
Elder Bednar called us to stay fully in the journey. In his talk "Ye Must Be Born Again," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

. . . After we come out of the waters of baptism, our souls need to be continuously immersed in and saturated with the truth and the light of the Savior’s gospel. Sporadic and shallow dipping in the doctrine of Christ and partial participation in His restored Church cannot produce the spiritual transformation that enables us to walk in a newness of life. Rather, fidelity to covenants, constancy of commitment, and offering our whole soul unto God are required if we are to receive the blessings of eternity. . . . Total immersion in and saturation with the Savior’s gospel are essential steps in the process of being born again.
Day hikes do not make you a mountaineer. A steady, committed climb does. That is what he is describing.
And Elder D. Todd Christofferson offered comfort for the weary. In his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference, he said:

You may ask, Why doesn’t this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
A process, not an event. The journey is the point. So be patient with the miles.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about their own baptism, or a baptism they saw. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Saul is baptized

blocks.text: Saul had been a fierce opponent of the Christians. On the road to Damascus, he met the risen Lord and was struck blind. A disciple named Ananias was sent to him, even though he was afraid.

And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost. And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received a sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.

He called him Brother Saul. A man who had come to arrest Christians was greeted as a brother. Saul could see again, and he was baptized. He became Paul, one of the greatest missionaries in history. His new path began with a single step into the water.

application.text: Here are a few ideas for this week.
Take a short walk, if you can. As you walk, think about the path you committed to at baptism. Where are you on it? What is the next step?
Write one sentence about what your baptism means to you. Keep it somewhere you will see. When the road feels long, read it.
Finally, walk beside someone. Is there a person who is struggling to keep going? Offer your company. That is exactly what Alma asked of the people at the waters of Mormon.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that baptism is the beginning of a path that leads to Christ. I know that He walked it first, and that He walks with us. I have felt the Holy Ghost help me when I was weary. I know that the Savior keeps His promises. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to take a short walk and think about the path you committed to at baptism. Where are you on it? What is your next step?
I invite you to write one sentence about what your baptism means to you, and keep it where you will see it.
I invite you to walk beside someone who is struggling to keep going, as Alma asked the people at the waters of Mormon.
blessings: You will see your next step more clearly.
You will have a reminder to read when the road feels long.
You will lighten someone's burden and find strength in doing it.

closingVerse.text: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
